triage.name: Warts
triage.reason: Common benign viral skin lesion with classic appearance; diagnosis is clinical and reachable by exam.

demographics: Common in school-age children and adolescents
More common in people who handle meat, fish or poultry for work
More common in people who share communal bathing or gym facilities

risk_factors.text: Close contact with someone who has warts
Walking barefoot in shared showers, pools or locker rooms
Occupational handling of meat, fish or poultry

comorbidities: Atopic dermatitis or other chronic skin conditions that break the skin barrier
social_history: Household member or close contact with warts
Participation in swimming or communal sports
exposures: Shared towels, razors or nail tools
Public showers, pool decks or gym floors

chief_complaints.text: I have a rough bump on my hand
There is a hard spot on the bottom of my foot that hurts when I walk
I keep getting more of these little bumps

hpi.onset: Gradual; a small rough bump appears and slowly enlarges over weeks
hpi.duration: Weeks to months; often present for a long time before the patient seeks care
hpi.progression: Slowly grows and may spread to nearby skin or to other family members; in children many warts clear on their own over months to a couple of years, while in adults they tend to persist
hpi.location: Most often on the hands, fingers and around the nails; also the soles of the feet, the face, and areas that are shaved
hpi.quality: Rough, raised, firm growth; plantar warts feel like a hard callus with a tender center
hpi.severity: Usually painless and only a cosmetic concern; plantar warts can be moderately painful with standing or walking
hpi.timing: Constant; plantar warts hurt most with direct pressure or walking
aggravating: Picking or biting at the wart
relieving: Offloading pressure from a plantar wart may ease the pain

associated_symptoms.text: Tiny black dots visible in the wart
A new wart appearing near an old one
Bleeding when the wart is knocked or picked

pertinent_negatives: Recent travel or sick contacts with a rash

positives.text: Rough, raised bump on the skin
Pain on walking or standing if the wart is on the sole

atypical.how_it_differs: Warts are very common and often multiple; many clear without treatment over months to a couple of years, so parents may report that the bumps come and go.
New warts are less common; a new rough growth in an older adult should be examined carefully because seborrheic keratoses and skin cancers can look similar.
Lesions are often numerous, larger, resistant to standard treatment and more likely to recur; they may spread widely.
Plantar warts may be mistaken for, or coexist with, diabetic foot calluses and ulcers; reduced sensation can delay noticing them and healing after treatment may be slower.
missing_classic_features: Pain as an early warning sign

general.mild: Well-appearing, comfortable, no distress; one or a few small skin lesions
general.moderate: Well-appearing; several lesions or a plantar wart causing mild discomfort with walking
general.severe: Well-appearing but uncomfortable; numerous or large lesions, or a plantar wart causing significant pain with weight-bearing
general.critical: Not applicable; warts are not a critical illness

findings.maneuver: Inspect the skin surface of the hands, fingers, feet and other exposed areas
findings.finding: Well-demarcated, raised, rough, hyperkeratotic papule or plaque with a verrucous (cauliflower-like) surface

findings.maneuver: Look closely at the surface of the lesion
findings.finding: Normal skin lines are interrupted or absent over the growth

findings.maneuver: Inspect the lesion with a hand lens or dermatoscope, or pare the surface
findings.finding: Tiny black dots (thrombosed capillaries) within the wart
Filiform or finger-like projections, often on the face or neck

findings.maneuver: Inspect the face, dorsa of hands and shaved areas
Inspect the nails and surrounding skin
findings.finding: Wart surrounding or under the nail plate, sometimes with nail dystrophy

findings.maneuver: Palpate or apply direct pressure to the lesion on the sole
findings.finding: Tenderness with direct pressure; pain with standing or walking

findings.maneuver: Inspect areas of prior trauma, shaving or scratching
findings.finding: New warts along a line of trauma

findings.maneuver: Assess general appearance and vital signs
findings.finding: No fever, no lymphadenopathy, no systemic illness

findings.maneuver: Inspect the lesion for asymmetry, irregular border, color variation, diameter >6 mm, or evolution
findings.finding: Absence of melanoma warning signs; lesion is uniform and verrucous
No spontaneous ulceration, crusting or bleeding

findings.text: Multiple small red-to-black dots (thrombosed capillaries) within a well-demarcated verrucous lesion
Interruption of normal skin markings over the lesion
Absence of pigment network, atypical vascular patterns or other features suggesting melanoma

imaging.study: Skin biopsy (punch or shave) with histopathology
imaging.preferred_when: Diagnosis is uncertain or malignancy is suspected

findings.text: Epidermal acanthosis, papillomatosis and hyperkeratosis with vertical columns of parakeratosis
Koilocytes (vacuolated squamous cells with shrunken nuclei) in the upper epidermis
Dilated capillaries with thrombosed vessels in the dermal papillae

initial.why: Diagnosis of warts is clinical; dermoscopy improves confidence by showing thrombosed capillaries and loss of skin lines

confirmatory.test: Skin biopsy (punch or shave) with histopathology
confirmatory.why: Confirms the diagnosis when the lesion is atypical or malignancy must be excluded
confirmatory.only_if: the diagnosis is uncertain, the lesion is changing, or malignancy is suspected

not_indicated.why: No role in a localized benign viral skin infection
No role in a localized benign viral skin infection
Warts do not cause systemic inflammation
Warts do not cause systemic inflammation
Not routinely needed for a typical wart; consider only if lesions are extensive, atypical or refractory
not_indicated.only_if: lesions are extensive, atypical or refractory to treatment

not_indicated.why: Not used to diagnose common cutaneous warts; reserved for cervical cancer screening or genital lesion evaluation
Used for herpes simplex or varicella-zoster, not warts

decision_points: Diagnose warts clinically; reserve biopsy for atypical, changing or non-responsive lesions
Consider immunodeficiency workup only if warts are extensive, atypical or refractory to standard therapy
Distinguish plantar warts from calluses and corns by loss of skin lines and thrombosed capillaries

differential.name: Squamous cell carcinoma
differential.why_considered: A rough, hyperkeratotic, sometimes tender growth on sun-exposed or previously damaged skin can look like a wart, especially in older adults.
differential.trigger: A rough keratotic growth in an older adult, or any wart-like lesion that is changing, ulcerating or bleeding

history: Rapid growth over weeks to months
Spontaneous ulceration, crusting or bleeding
Older age or extensive sun exposure
History of prior skin cancer or actinic damage
exam: Indurated base or rolled, everted border
Friable, easily bleeding surface
Fixation to underlying tissue
Regional lymphadenopathy
labs: No specific blood test; diagnosis is by biopsy
imaging: Skin biopsy showing invasive atypical squamous cells
Dermoscopy showing polymorphous vessels, keratin masses and no thrombosed capillaries

differential.name: Melanoma
differential.why_considered: A new or changing pigmented lesion on the hands or feet can be mistaken for a wart, particularly acral and subungual melanoma.
differential.trigger: A pigmented lesion with asymmetry, irregular border, color variation, diameter over 6 mm, or evolution, especially on the palm, sole or under a nail

history: Change in size, shape, color or symptoms over weeks to months
Bleeding or itching without trauma
Personal or family history of melanoma
exam: Asymmetric lesion with irregular, notched border
Multiple colors including black, brown, red or blue
Longitudinal nail streak (Hutchinson sign) if subungual
Absence of the verrucous, cauliflower-like surface
labs: No specific blood test; diagnosis is by biopsy
imaging: Dermoscopy showing atypical pigment network, irregular streaks or blue-white veil
Excisional biopsy with histopathology confirming melanocytes

differential.name: Seborrheic keratosis
differential.why_considered: A raised, rough, sometimes pigmented growth that can resemble a wart, especially on the trunk and in older adults.

history: Slowly enlarging over years
Often multiple similar lesions elsewhere
Usually asymptomatic
exam: Well-demarcated, 'stuck-on' appearance
Waxy, verrucous or smooth surface with comedo-like openings
No thrombosed capillaries
Normal skin lines preserved over the lesion
imaging: Dermoscopy showing milia-like cysts, comedo-like openings and a sharp border
Biopsy only if atypical or changing

differential.name: Callus or corn
differential.why_considered: A painful, hard thickening on the sole of the foot is a common reason patients think they have a plantar wart.

history: Related to pressure or friction from shoes or activity
No spread to other sites
No household contacts with warts
exam: Normal skin lines continue through the lesion
No thrombosed capillaries or black dots
Pain with direct pressure but no pinpoint tenderness
Paring reveals uniform hyperkeratosis without bleeding points

differential.name: Molluscum contagiosum
differential.why_considered: Another common viral skin infection in children that causes multiple small bumps and can spread by contact.

history: Small, smooth, dome-shaped bumps rather than rough growths
Spread by close contact or shared items
Often in children or immunocompromised patients
exam: Flesh-colored, dome-shaped papules with central umbilication
No verrucous surface or black dots
Usually 2–5 mm in size
imaging: Dermoscopy showing central pore and lobulated white-yellow structure

differential.name: Herpes simplex
differential.why_considered: A recurrent vesicular or ulcerated lesion on the skin or mucosa can be confused with a wart, especially near the mouth or genitals.

history: Prodrome of tingling, burning or itching
Recurrent grouped blisters that rupture and crust
Triggered by stress, illness or sun exposure
exam: Grouped vesicles on an erythematous base
Superficial ulcerations with scalloped borders
No rough, keratotic surface
labs: Positive HSV PCR or viral culture from a swab of the lesion
Tzanck smear showing multinucleated giant cells

differential.name: Fifth disease (erythema infectiosum)
differential.why_considered: A common childhood viral exanthem that can cause a rash on the hands and feet, though the morphology is different from warts.

history: Prodromal low-grade fever and malaise
Slapped-cheek facial rash followed by lacy reticular rash on extremities
Resolves over 1–3 weeks
exam: Diffuse erythematous rash, not discrete rough papules
No hyperkeratosis or thrombosed capillaries
No localized verrucous growth
labs: Parvovirus B19 IgM or PCR if needed
No specific test required for typical presentation

severity.mild: One or a few small, asymptomatic warts that do not interfere with daily activities; often noticed incidentally or for cosmetic reasons.
severity.moderate: Multiple warts or a plantar wart causing mild discomfort with walking or standing; may be spreading to nearby skin.
severity.severe: Numerous, large or confluent warts causing significant pain, functional limitation or marked cosmetic concern; often refractory to initial treatment.
severity.critical: Not applicable; warts are not a life-threatening condition.

red_flags.finding: Rapid growth, ulceration, bleeding or change in color
red_flags.meaning: Suggests malignancy such as squamous cell carcinoma or melanoma; biopsy is needed

red_flags.finding: Lesion on the sole or palm with atypical pigmentation or nail involvement

red_flags.meaning: Consider underlying immunodeficiency such as HIV or immunosuppressive therapy

red_flags.finding: New rough growth in an older adult without prior warts
red_flags.meaning: Seborrheic keratosis or skin cancer is more likely; examine carefully

red_flags.finding: Signs of secondary bacterial infection (increased pain, redness, pus, fever)
red_flags.meaning: Secondary cellulitis or abscess; may need antibiotics or drainage

complications.name: Spread to adjacent skin or other body sites
clues: New warts appearing near the original lesion

complications.name: Pain or functional limitation from plantar warts
clues: Altered gait to offload the affected foot

complications.name: Secondary bacterial infection
clues: Increasing redness, warmth, swelling or purulent drainage

complications.name: Scarring or dyspigmentation after treatment
clues: History of cryotherapy, laser or surgical removal
Visible scar or color change at treatment site

complications.name: Nail dystrophy from periungual warts
clues: Wart surrounding or under the nail
Nail plate ridging, splitting or distortion

special_populations.differences: Warts are very common and often multiple; many clear spontaneously over months to a couple of years, so observation is a reasonable first step. Treatment may be deferred unless painful or spreading.
New warts are less common; a new rough growth should be examined carefully because seborrheic keratoses and skin cancers can look similar. Biopsy threshold should be lower.
Lesions are often numerous, larger, resistant to standard treatment and more likely to recur. They may spread widely and require more aggressive or combination therapy.
Plantar warts may be mistaken for, or coexist with, diabetic foot calluses and ulcers. Reduced sensation can delay noticing them, and healing after treatment may be slower.
Warts may increase in size or number due to immune changes. Many treatments are avoided or used with caution; cryotherapy and some topical agents are considered safer than others.

key_questions.question: What does the bump look like, and how has it changed since you first noticed it?
key_questions.looking_for: A rough, raised, slowly enlarging growth over weeks to months; rapid change, ulceration or bleeding points away from a wart

key_questions.question: When did it first appear, and has it spread to other areas?
key_questions.looking_for: Gradual onset over weeks to months with possible spread to nearby skin or new lesions elsewhere

key_questions.question: Where on your body is it located?
key_questions.looking_for: Hands, fingers, around the nails, soles of the feet, face, or shaved areas

key_questions.question: Does it hurt, itch or bleed?
key_questions.looking_for: Usually painless; plantar warts hurt with pressure or walking; bleeding or itching without trauma is concerning

key_questions.question: Have you or anyone close to you had warts before?
key_questions.looking_for: Household or close contact with warts, supporting contagious spread

key_questions.question: Do you walk barefoot in shared showers, pools or locker rooms, or handle meat, fish or poultry for work?
key_questions.looking_for: Exposures that increase the risk of HPV skin infection

key_questions.question: Do you bite your nails, pick at your cuticles or shave over the area?
key_questions.looking_for: Behaviors that break the skin barrier and promote autoinoculation

key_questions.question: Have you tried any treatments, and did they help?
key_questions.looking_for: Prior over-the-counter salicylic acid, cryotherapy or other treatments and their response

key_questions.question: Do you have a condition or take a medication that weakens your immune system?
key_questions.looking_for: HIV, transplant, chemotherapy or immunosuppressant use, which can cause extensive or refractory warts

key_questions.question: Is there any chance this could be a genital or sexually transmitted lesion?
key_questions.looking_for: Genital warts or other STI, which changes counseling and screening

key_questions.question: Have you noticed any fever, weight loss, night sweats or feeling unwell?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent; systemic symptoms argue against a simple wart

key_questions.question: Has the lesion changed color, become asymmetric, or developed irregular borders?
key_questions.looking_for: Features concerning for melanoma or squamous cell carcinoma, requiring biopsy

reasoning_points: A rough, raised, hyperkeratotic papule or plaque with a verrucous surface on the hands, feet or other exposed skin
Gradual onset and slow enlargement over weeks to months without systemic symptoms
Interruption of normal skin lines over the lesion and tiny black dots (thrombosed capillaries)
Plantar warts cause pain with direct pressure or walking and lack normal skin lines
Risk factors such as close contact with warts, skin breaks, communal bathing areas or occupational meat handling
No fever, lymphadenopathy or other systemic illness
Absence of melanoma or squamous cell carcinoma warning signs; biopsy reserved for atypical or changing lesions
Diagnosis is clinical, supported by dermoscopy when needed

easy: School-age child with a rough, cauliflower-like bump on the hand
Classic verrucous surface with black dots and loss of skin lines
No systemic symptoms and a clear history of a household contact with warts
medium: Plantar wart mistaken for a callus or corn; pain with pressure and loss of skin lines help distinguish
Multiple flat warts in a shaved area
Adult with a single persistent wart and no spontaneous clearance
hard: Older adult with a new rough growth that could be a seborrheic keratosis or squamous cell carcinoma
Pigmented lesion on the palm or sole or under a nail raising concern for acral or subungual melanoma
Immunocompromised patient with numerous, large or treatment-resistant warts
Diabetic patient with a plantar lesion that could be a callus, ulcer or wart
Lesion that has ulcerated or bled without trauma, requiring biopsy
